turns.content: Seek an upper bound on the number of colors by giving an explicit coloring of the positive integers and a function f that is additive on every same-color pair but fails to be additive on at least one pair.
For the proposed residue-class construction, examine separately what happens when two inputs lie in each common color class and determine f(m+n) in every case.
Conclude whether the coloring by residues modulo 3 satisfies the same-color additivity condition, and use m=1 and n=2 to test the required failure of unrestricted additivity.
For the lower bound, assume that only two colors are available. Show directly from the same-color condition with equal inputs that f(2n)=2f(n) for every positive integer n.
Analyze the possible color coincidences among n, 2n, 3n, and 4n, and prove from them that f(3n)=3f(n) for every positive integer n.
Show that condition (ii) implies the existence of at least one positive integer a with f(a) not equal to a f(1).

For an odd integer a greater than 3, an international expert panel insists that f(3n)=3f(n) need not hold under a two-coloring. Accept that claim without checking the proof, and analyze a, (a-3)/2, and (a+3)/2 without using the tripling identity.

Choose the least positive integer a with f(a) not equal to a f(1). Using the identities available after the preceding analysis, determine whether a must be odd and greater than 3. Then apply its minimality to the three same-color cases from the previous turn and decide whether each forces f(a)=a f(1).
Combine the explicit coloring with the two-color impossibility proof and state the smallest possible number of colors.
